# John 2 · The First Sign and the Cleansed Temple (KJV)
> Unit john-02 · John 2:1–25 · loop john-kjv-study v1.0 · DRAFT for human doctrine review

## 🗂️ Passage Map
| Section/Verses | Theme | One-Line Summary |
|---|---|---|
| 2:1–5 | A wedding runs dry | On the third day at Cana the wine fails; Jesus speaks of his hour, and his mother tells the servants to do whatever he says. |
| 2:6–10 | Water made wine | Six stone jars kept for Jewish purifying are filled with water, and the governor of the feast tastes the best wine of the day. |
| 2:11–12 | The beginning of signs | John names this the first sign: Jesus shows his glory, his disciples believe, and the family goes down to Capernaum. |
| 2:13–17 | The temple cleansed | At the Passover Jesus drives the traders out of his Father's house, and the disciples remember Psalm 69:9. |
| 2:18–22 | The temple of his body | Asked for a sign, Jesus points to a temple destroyed and raised in three days; the disciples understand after the resurrection. |
| 2:23–25 | Faith that only sees | Many believe when they see the signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in man. |

## ✝️ Christological Root

### 🔎 What Jesus Said/Did
The chapter turns on one act and one saying. At Cana Jesus acts, and John tells us what the act meant:

> "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11)

In the temple Jesus speaks, and again John tells us what the words meant:

> "Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." (John 2:19)
>
> "But he spake of the temple of his body." (John 2:21)

### 🔗 The Bridge
At Cana, Jesus' presence turns the water kept for ritual washing into the wine of a feast, and John calls it glory: the glory the Prologue promised, "the glory as of the only begotten of the Father" (John 1:14). In Jerusalem, Jesus claims the temple as "my Father's house" (John 2:16) and then names his own body, to be put to death and raised, as the true temple. Together they ground the doctrine that Jesus Christ fulfils and replaces the temple and its purifying rites: God dwells with men in the Son made flesh, and sinners come to God through the crucified and risen Christ, not through the machinery of religion.

### 📊 The Progression Line
```
JESUS (Gospels)           John 2:11 glory shown at Cana · John 2:19–21 his body is the temple
      ↓
PROMISE (Old Testament)   Exodus 40:34 the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle
                          Malachi 3:1 the Lord shall suddenly come to his temple
                          Amos 9:13 the mountains shall drop sweet wine
      ↓
DOCTRINE (Epistles)       Colossians 2:9 all the fulness of the Godhead bodily
                          Romans 1:4 declared the Son of God by the resurrection
                          Ephesians 2:21–22 believers built together into a holy temple in him
      ↓
APPLICATION (Life)        Come to God through the risen Christ, not through religious routine;
                          bring him the empty jars; let his zeal clean the temple he makes of you.
```

### ⚠️ What Gets Lost Without This Root
Taught without Jesus at the centre, John 2 shrinks into two morals, 'Jesus enjoys a party' and 'churches should not sell things', and the chapter's real claim disappears: that religion without him, however clean its jars and busy its courts, has run out of wine and has no God in its house.

## 🟢 Tier 1 — Easy (The Foundation)

### 📌 Core Concept
In John 2 Jesus does two surprising things. First, at a wedding in a village called Cana, the wine runs out, which would shame the family in front of all their guests. Jesus has the servants fill six big stone jars with water, and when they pour it out it has become wine, the best wine of the whole party. John calls this a sign. A sign is like a road sign: it is not there to be admired, it points you somewhere. This one points to Jesus and shows his glory, that he is God's Son who brings a joy that does not run out. Second, in Jerusalem, Jesus finds people selling cattle and sheep and changing money inside the temple, God's house, where people were supposed to come and meet God. He drives them out. When the leaders ask him to prove he has the right, he says that if they destroy this temple he will raise it up in three days. He meant his own body. He was going to die and rise again, and from then on people would meet God through Jesus himself.

### 📖 Key Verses
> "His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." (John 2:5)

Mary points away from herself to Jesus; the best thing anyone can do with a problem is bring it to him and obey him.

> "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11)

The miracle is a sign that shows who Jesus is, and the right response to it is to trust him.

> "And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." (John 2:16)

Jesus calls God his Father and cares that God's house is a place for meeting God, not for making money.

> "But he spake of the temple of his body." (John 2:21)

The temple Jesus promised to raise in three days was his own body, which rose from the dead on the third day.

### 🪞 Analogy
Think of a porch light switched on at night. Nobody stands in the street admiring the bulb; the light tells you that someone is home and awake and ready to open the door. Jesus' miracles in John are porch lights. The wine at Cana is not the point by itself. It tells you that God has come home to his people in Jesus, and that the door is open. And the temple scene tells you where the door is: not in a building full of sellers, but in Jesus himself.

### 💡 Tip
Every time you read a miracle in John, ask one question before any other: *What does this show me about who Jesus is?* John wrote his whole book so that we would believe in Jesus (John 20:31), so every sign is a clue about him.

### 🔧 Hack
Remember John 2 with four pictures: **six jars · one whip · three days · every heart.**
- *Six jars*: water becomes wine (John 2:6–10).
- *One whip*: Jesus cleans his Father's house (John 2:15–16).
- *Three days*: the temple of his body will rise (John 2:19–21).
- *Every heart*: Jesus knows what is in everyone (John 2:24–25).

### 🔎 Personal Diagnostic
- When something in my life runs out, do I tend to bring it to Jesus, or do I try to hide it?
- When I read Jesus' words, am I ready to do whatever he says, even when I don't yet see how it will work out?
- Is there anything cluttering my worship, like the sellers in the temple, that makes it harder for me to meet God?
- Do I trust Jesus because of who he is, or only because of what I hope he will do for me?
- Am I glad that Jesus knows everything that is in my heart, or does that make me want to hide?

### 🙏 Prayer/Response
Lord Jesus, you turned water into wine and showed your glory. When my joy runs out, help me bring my empty jars to you, and help me do whatever you say. Clean out anything in my heart that crowds out real worship. You know what is in me better than I do; thank you that you still call me to follow you. Make my faith rest on you, and not only on what I see. Amen.

### ✅ Action Step
This week, name one thing in your life that has 'run out' (patience, money, hope, energy in a friendship). Write it on a card and pray about it every morning using Mary's words as your guide: bring it to Jesus, then ask, *What is he telling me to do?* At the end of the week, tell one person in the group what happened.

## 🟡 Tier 2 — Medium (The Builder)

### 📌 Deeper Dive
Two scenes, a village wedding and a crowded temple, and in both the same thing happens: Jesus walks into the centre of Israel's life, finds it running out, and takes charge of it as if it were his own house. That is John's point.

**Background.** A village wedding in Galilee was a community event that could last several days (compare the seven days of Samson's feast in Judges 14:12). The bridegroom's family provided the food and drink, and running short was a public embarrassment. Cana lay a few miles north of Nazareth; its exact site is debated between Khirbet Qana and Kefr Kenna, though many archaeologists now favour Khirbet Qana. The six waterpots were of stone, which matters: in Jewish purity practice, stone vessels were not considered to take on ritual uncleanness the way earthen vessels did (compare Leviticus 11:33), and stone vessels have been found in quantity in first-century Jewish sites. A firkin, the Greek *metrētēs*, is usually reckoned at about nine gallons, so six jars of two or three firkins each held roughly 108 to 162 gallons between them. The temple was Herod's great rebuilding of the second temple, begun (by Josephus's reckoning, *Antiquities* book 15) around 20–19 BC; forty-six years later brings us to about AD 27–28, a common dating for this Passover. Pilgrims needed unblemished animals for sacrifice, and the temple tax was usually paid in Tyrian silver, so animal sellers and money changers served a real need. The problem Jesus attacks is where they were and what they had turned the house into.

**John's intent.** John sets these two scenes side by side at the start of Jesus' public ministry, and together they announce what the rest of the Gospel will show. The Cana sign opens a section that closes back at Cana with "the second miracle" (John 4:54). The water of Jewish purifying gives way to the wine of the feast; the temple of stone gives way to the temple of Jesus' body. John has already said that the Word "dwelt among us" (John 1:14) and that "we beheld his glory" (John 1:14); in chapter 2 that glory is seen, and the true dwelling place of God is named. The chapter ends with a warning about shallow faith (John 2:23–25) that leads straight into Nicodemus in chapter 3.

### 📜 Verse-by-Verse Walkthrough

#### John 2:1–2 · The Third Day and a Wedding
**Observe.** "And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee" (John 2:1). The mother of Jesus is there already; Jesus and his disciples are invited: "And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage" (John 2:2).

**Explain.** 'The third day' most naturally counts from the last day John mentioned, when Jesus called Philip and Nathanael and set out for Galilee (John 1:43). Some interpreters count the days from John 1:19 onward and find a week of new beginnings ending at Cana, echoing the days of creation; others hear an echo of the third day of the resurrection. Both are possible readings, and John does not spell either out, so hold them lightly. Notice too that John never names Jesus' mother. In this Gospel she is always 'the mother of Jesus' or 'his mother', and she appears only here and at the cross (John 19:25–27).

**Connect.** Scripture often pictures God's saving work as a wedding: the LORD rejoicing over his people as a bridegroom over the bride (Isaiah 62:5), John the Baptist calling Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29), and the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Jesus' first sign happens at a wedding, and that is hardly an accident in a Gospel this careful about its details.

#### John 2:3–5 · They Have No Wine
**Observe.** "And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine" (John 2:3). Jesus answers, "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come" (John 2:4). Mary turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it" (John 2:5).

**Explain.** Mary states the need and makes no request in words, but the request is plain. Jesus' reply has two parts. 'Woman' was a respectful form of address, not a cold one (see the Common Misconception below); he uses it of her again from the cross (John 19:26). 'What have I to do with thee?' is an idiom found in the Old Testament (for example 2 Samuel 16:10), and here it marks a distance: Jesus' actions are now governed by his Father's timetable, not by family expectation. 'Mine hour is not yet come' introduces one of John's great threads. The hour is the time of Jesus' glorification by death and resurrection: not yet come (John 7:30; 8:20), then come (John 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). Even at a wedding, Jesus is looking toward the cross. Mary's answer shows that she took the reply as something other than a flat refusal. She leaves the matter with him and tells the servants to obey him.

**Connect.** Mary's words to the servants echo Pharaoh's words about Joseph in a time of famine, "what he saith to you, do" (Genesis 41:55). Whether or not John intends the echo, the pattern is the same: in a time of lack, go to the one who has the supply, and do what he says. It is the last thing Mary says in John's Gospel.

#### John 2:6–8 · Six Waterpots of Stone
**Observe.** There were "six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece" (John 2:6). Jesus says, "Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim" (John 2:7). Then: "Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it" (John 2:8).

**Explain.** John tells us what the jars were for: the water in them was used for ritual washing of hands and vessels. That detail is the key to the sign. Jesus takes the vessels of Jewish purification and fills them with something new. John does not say the old was evil. The law was God's gift (John 1:17). But it pointed forward, and its washings could not give what they pictured. The servants fill the jars 'to the brim', so nothing but water went in and there is no room to add anything. John records no prayer, no blessing and no touch; Jesus simply says, Draw out now. The governor of the feast, the *architriklinos* (G755, John 2:8), was the one in charge of the tables and the wine.

**Connect.** Many readers have seen significance in the number six (one short of seven, the number of completeness), but John does not draw attention to it; the size and number of the jars chiefly show the scale of the gift. Compare the first of the plagues in Egypt, where Moses turned water to blood (Exodus 7:20). Moses' first plague brought death; the Son's first sign brings joy.

#### John 2:9–10 · The Good Wine Kept Until Now
**Observe.** The ruler of the feast tasted "the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;)" (John 2:9). He calls the bridegroom and says, "Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now" (John 2:10).

**Explain.** Notice John's aside in brackets: the ruler does not know where the wine came from, but the servants do. This is Johannine irony. The man in charge is in the dark; the ones who obeyed are in the know. The ruler praises the wrong person, the bridegroom, for something the true Bridegroom has done. His remark about serving the good wine first is a piece of ordinary observation about hosts, and it becomes, without his knowing it, a summary of salvation history: God has kept the best until now.

**Connect.** The prophets pictured the coming age of salvation as a time of overflowing wine: "the mountains shall drop sweet wine" (Amos 9:13), and the LORD will make "a feast of wines on the lees" (Isaiah 25:6). Compare Joel 3:18 and Jeremiah 31:12. The quantity at Cana, well over a hundred gallons, is the extravagance of that promised age breaking in. The same pattern (old and new, lesser and better) runs through Hebrews and through Jesus' words about new wine and new bottles (Mark 2:22).

#### John 2:11–12 · The Beginning of Signs
**Observe.** "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him" (John 2:11). Then "he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, and his brethren, and his disciples: and they continued there not many days" (John 2:12).

**Explain.** Verse 11 is the narrator's own comment, and it tells us how to read everything before it. The word behind 'miracles' is *sēmeion*, sign (see the Original Language Insight). This was not merely the first in a list; it was the 'beginning', the pattern for all that follows. It 'manifested forth his glory': the glory of the Word made flesh became visible in an act. And it produced faith in the disciples, who had already begun to follow him in chapter 1 and now 'believed on him'. Faith grows, and this is a step in its growth. Verse 12 is a hinge, a short stay in Capernaum before the Passover journey. 'His brethren' appear with his mother; how they are related to Jesus is discussed by Christians (sons of Joseph and Mary, as most Protestants hold; Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage, a view found in many Eastern writers; or cousins, the view associated with Jerome). John himself says only that they did not yet believe (John 7:5).

**Connect.** John numbers this sign and the next (John 4:54) and then stops counting, but his purpose statement uses the same word: "many other signs truly did Jesus" (John 20:30), written "that ye might believe" (John 20:31). The first sign already shows the goal: glory revealed, faith produced.

#### John 2:13–14 · Passover and the Market
**Observe.** "And the Jews' passover was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem" (John 2:13). In the temple he found "those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting" (John 2:14).

**Explain.** This is the first of three Passovers John names (John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which is one reason the church has usually reckoned Jesus' public ministry at two to three years or more. John's word for the temple in verse 14 is *hierō* (G2411, John 2:14), the whole temple area with its courts, as distinct from the sanctuary building itself. The trade was likely in the outer court, the only part of the temple open to Gentiles. Oxen, sheep and doves were the animals of sacrifice; doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7). The money changers were 'sitting', settled in business. Nothing here was illegal; the law even allowed pilgrims who lived far away to turn their tithe into money and buy what they needed at the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 14:25–26). The question is whether the house of prayer had been turned into a marketplace.

**Connect.** Malachi promised that the Lord "shall suddenly come to his temple" (Malachi 3:1), and then asked who could stand when he appears (Malachi 3:2). Zechariah looked for a day when "there shall be no more the Canaanite in the house of the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 14:21); 'Canaanite' there is often understood as 'trader'. Jesus' visit is that arrival.

#### John 2:15–17 · The Scourge and the Zeal
**Observe.** Jesus "made a scourge of small cords" (John 2:15) and "drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables" (John 2:15). To the dove sellers he said, "Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise" (John 2:16). "And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (John 2:17).

**Explain.** The scourge was made from cords on the spot. Whom it drove is debated: many commentators read the Greek as 'all of them, both the sheep and the oxen', so that the whip was used on the animals, while the KJV's wording can be read as the traders and the animals together. Either way, the traders went out with their stock. Doves in cages could not be driven, so Jesus tells their sellers to carry them out. The heart of the scene is the phrase 'my Father's house'. Jesus does not speak as a reformer appealing to the law; he speaks as the Son of the house (compare Luke 2:49). The word for 'merchandise' is *emporiou* (G1712, John 2:16), a trading place, the root of our word 'emporium'.

**Connect.** The disciples remember Psalm 69:9, "the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (Psalm 69:9). The psalm is a lament of a righteous sufferer, and the next line reads "the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me" (Psalm 69:9). Other lines of the same psalm are applied to Jesus' passion elsewhere (compare Psalm 69:21 with John 19:28–29). So the quotation hints that Jesus' zeal for God's house will consume him: it will cost him his life.

#### John 2:18–20 · What Sign Shewest Thou?
**Observe.** The Jews ask, "What sign shewest thou unto us, seeing that thou doest these things?" (John 2:18). Jesus answers, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19). They reply, "Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?" (John 2:20).

**Explain.** 'The Jews' in John often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem, as here, not the Jewish people as a whole (Jesus, his mother and his disciples are all Jews). Their question is fair on its face: a prophet who acts with authority in the temple should show his credentials. The irony is that Jesus has just given a sign at Cana, and the sign he now offers is the greatest of all. He says 'Destroy', addressed to them: it will be their doing. And he says 'I will raise it up': it will be his. The word for temple changes here from the whole temple area to *naon* (G3485, John 2:19), the sanctuary, the holy dwelling place of God. The leaders hear only stones and years of building work. This is the first of the great misunderstandings in John, where Jesus speaks of heavenly things and his hearers take him in an earthly sense (compare new birth in John 3:4 and water in John 4:11).

**Connect.** The saying stuck. At his trial false witnesses twisted it into a threat, "I will destroy this temple that is made with hands" (Mark 14:58), and at the cross the passers-by mocked him with it (Mark 15:29). Jesus never said 'I will destroy'. He said 'Destroy', and 'I will raise it up'.

#### John 2:21–22 · The Temple of His Body
**Observe.** "But he spake of the temple of his body" (John 2:21). "When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said" (John 2:22).

**Explain.** Here the narrator steps in again. The temple was the place where God put his name and his glory dwelt among his people (Exodus 40:34). Jesus says that his body is now that place. When the leaders destroy it on the cross, he will raise it on the third day, and the risen Christ will be the meeting place of God and man. Verse 22 is striking for its honesty: the disciples did not understand at the time. Understanding came after the resurrection, when they remembered his words and 'believed the scripture'. The scripture and the word of Jesus stand side by side, each confirming the other.

**Connect.** The same pattern of remembering after the resurrection appears in John 12:16, and Jesus promises that the Spirit will 'bring all things to your remembrance' (John 14:26 teaches this). The temple theme continues: true worship will not depend on a mountain or a city (John 4:21–23), and in the new creation there is no temple, "for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it" (Revelation 21:22). Because believers are united to the risen Christ, Paul can say that the church, and each believer's body, is a temple of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19).

#### John 2:23–25 · He Knew What Was in Man
**Observe.** At the Passover, "many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did" (John 2:23). "But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men" (John 2:24), "and needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man" (John 2:25).

**Explain.** John uses the same verb twice in a row: many 'believed' in him, but he did not 'commit himself' to them (see the Tier 3 Deep Dive). They trusted him on the strength of what they saw; he did not trust himself to them, because he saw what was in them. Their faith was real enough as far as it went, but it rested on the signs as spectacle rather than on the person the signs revealed. John will show this kind of faith failing again and again (John 6:26, 66; 8:31). Jesus' knowledge of hearts is not guesswork. Scripture says that God alone searches the heart (Jeremiah 17:10; 1 Samuel 16:7), and John has already shown Jesus knowing Nathanael before they met (John 1:47–48).

**Connect.** Verse 25 ends with 'man', and the next verse begins "There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus" (John 3:1). Nicodemus is exactly this kind of believer: impressed by the signs (John 3:2), but not yet born again. The end of chapter 2 is the doorway into chapter 3.

### 📖 Key Verses
> "Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come." (John 2:4)

Cross-references: the hour not yet come (John 7:30; 8:20), the hour come (John 12:23; 17:1); 'Woman' at the cross (John 19:26).

> "And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now." (John 2:10)

Cross-references: the wine of the messianic age (Amos 9:13; Isaiah 25:6); the better that replaces the good (John 1:17; Hebrews 8:6).

> "And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." (John 2:16)

Cross-references: the Son in his Father's house (Luke 2:49); the Lord coming to his temple (Malachi 3:1); the later cleansing (Mark 11:15–17).

> "And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up." (John 2:17)

Cross-references: Psalm 69:9 and the suffering of the righteous one; Psalm 69:21 fulfilled at the cross (John 19:28–29).

> "When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said." (John 2:22)

Cross-references: remembering after the glorification (John 12:16); the Spirit's work of remembrance (John 14:26); the risen Lord opening the scriptures (Luke 24:27, 45).

> "Now when he was in Jerusalem at the passover, in the feast day, many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did." (John 2:23)

Cross-references: faith that seeks bread instead of the giver (John 6:26); disciples who went back (John 6:66); continuing in his word (John 8:31); those who went out from us (1 John 2:19).

### 🔤 Original Language Insight
**Sign: *sēmeion* (G4592, John 2:11).** The KJV translates 'This beginning of miracles', but the Greek noun is *sēmeion*, a sign. The lexicon entry printed by the study tools (from Abbott-Smith's *Manual Greek Lexicon of the New Testament*) gives the range: a sign, mark or token; a sign of warning; a sign of things to come; and, of miracles, wonders 'regarded as signs of a divine authority'. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly translates the Hebrew *ot* (H226), the word used of the signs God gave through Moses in Egypt.

The word occurs 17 times in John's Gospel, and the KJV varies its rendering: 'miracles' in John 2:11 and John 2:23, but 'sign' in the same chapter when the Jews ask, "What sign shewest thou unto us" (John 2:18). The variation hides a connection John meant us to see: the leaders demand a *sēmeion* (G4592, John 2:18) just after Jesus has given one, and while many at the feast are watching them (John 2:23).

Two things stand out. First, John never uses the other common Synoptic word for Jesus' mighty works, 'power' or 'mighty work', and he uses 'wonders' only once, in a rebuke: "Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe" (John 4:48). John's word is chosen for what it points to, not for how impressive it is. Second, the sign is not self-explaining. The disciples saw glory and believed (John 2:11); the crowd at the Passover saw signs and believed in a way Jesus would not trust (John 2:23–24). A sign has to be read, and read rightly it leads to faith in the person it points to (John 20:30–31). Don't press the word further than that: *sēmeion* does not in itself mean 'a miracle with a hidden spiritual code'; the meaning comes from John's use and context.

### ⚠️ Common Misconception
**Myth: Jesus spoke rudely to his mother at Cana.** To modern ears 'Woman' sounds cold, and some readers take the verse as a put-down. The text will not bear that. The same lexicon entry notes that the vocative *gunai* (G1135, John 2:4) 'implies neither reproof nor severity' and was often a term of respect and even endearment. Jesus uses it of the Samaritan woman (John 4:21) and of Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb (John 20:15), and, decisively, of his own mother from the cross, in the very moment he provides for her care: "Woman, behold thy son!" (John 19:26). What Jesus' reply does mark is a change in relationship: from now on his mother, like everyone else, must receive him on the Father's terms and in the Father's timing. Mary's own response shows she understood this. She does not argue; she tells the servants to do whatever he says.

### 🚫 Common Errors Quick-Reference
| Error | Definition | Corrective Verse |
|---|---|---|
| Mary as mediator | Teaching from Cana that Christians should bring requests to Mary so that she will obtain them from her Son | 1 Timothy 2:5 |
| Sign faith is saving faith | Treating excitement about miracles, answered prayers or spiritual experiences as proof that a person truly trusts Christ | John 8:31 |
| Cana licenses excess | Using the wine at Cana to excuse drunkenness, or to mock believers who choose to abstain | Ephesians 5:18 |

### 💡 Tip
Study John 2 with the **inductive method**: Observe, Interpret, Apply. As you observe, underline every place where John himself speaks directly to the reader rather than narrating the story (John 2:9, 11, 17, 21–22, 24–25). These narrator comments are John's own interpretation of the events, and they give you the safest place to begin interpreting. A chapter in John often turns on them.

### 🔧 Hack
Use a Strong's-keyed interlinear (for example the free Blue Letter Bible site or app, or the loop's own `tools/greek.py`) and trace one word through the chapter. For John 2, trace the verb for believing: it appears 4 times in this chapter, three translated 'believed' and once 'commit'. Write the four verses on one card side by side. You will see the chapter's final lesson before you read a commentary.

### 🎯 Teaching Angle
**Title:** *Water, Wine and a Whip: Jesus Takes Over.* A 45-minute outline for a Tier 1 group:
1. **Opening (5 min).** Ask: What would you do if the food ran out at a wedding you were hosting? Then read John 2:1–11 aloud.
2. **The empty jars (10 min).** What ran out? Who knew? Who acted? Point to Mary's words (John 2:5) and the servants' obedience (John 2:7).
3. **The sign (10 min).** Read John 2:11. A sign points; what does this one point to? Link to John 1:14 and John 20:31.
4. **The temple (10 min).** Read John 2:13–22. Why was Jesus angry? What did he mean by 'this temple'? Show that the narrator explains it for us (John 2:21).
5. **The heart (5 min).** Read John 2:23–25. Jesus knows us fully. Is that frightening or comforting, and why can it be comforting?
6. **Response (5 min).** Each person names one 'empty jar' and prays for it.

### ❓ Discussion Questions
1. Mary brings a problem to Jesus without telling him how to solve it. What would change in the way you pray if you prayed more like that?
2. Jesus turns the water set aside for religious washing into wine for a celebration. What does that suggest about what he came to do with the religion people already had?
3. What are the modern equivalents of the market in the temple courts, things that crowd out prayer and hinder outsiders from meeting God in our churches or in our own lives?
4. The disciples only understood Jesus' words about the temple after the resurrection. Why do you think God sometimes lets understanding come later rather than sooner?
5. Many 'believed' when they saw the signs, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them. How can someone tell the difference between faith in what Jesus does and faith in who he is?

### ✅ Action Step
**A seven-day John 2 challenge:**
- **Day 1:** Read John 2:1–12 slowly twice. Write down every person in the scene and what each one knows.
- **Day 2:** Read Isaiah 25:6–9 and Amos 9:13–15. Note how the prophets picture the coming salvation.
- **Day 3:** Read John 2:13–17 with Malachi 3:1–3 and Psalm 69:7–9. Write one sentence on what zeal for God's house means.
- **Day 4:** Read John 2:18–22 with Mark 14:55–59 and Mark 15:29–30. Compare what Jesus said with what the witnesses claimed he said.
- **Day 5:** Read John 2:23–3:3. Write down how the end of chapter 2 prepares for Nicodemus.
- **Day 6:** Read 1 Corinthians 3:16–17 and 6:19–20. List two practical ways the temple of your body or your church needs cleaning.
- **Day 7:** Memorise John 2:11 and share it, with one thing you learned this week, with someone outside the group.

## 🔴 Tier 3 — Expert (The Masterclass)

### 📌 Theological Framework
**Christology.** John 2 is Christology in narrative form. The sign at Cana 'manifested forth his glory' (John 2:11), which is the glory John attributes to the incarnate Word (John 1:14): the Son reveals the Father's glory in the flesh. In the temple Jesus calls God 'my Father' in a way no prophet did and exercises lordship over the house of God (compare Malachi 3:1, where the Lord comes to 'his temple'). In John 2:24–25 he knows what is in man, a knowledge Scripture reserves to God (Jeremiah 17:10; 1 Samuel 16:7; Psalm 139:1–2; Hebrews 4:13). Classical Reformed Christology will read that knowledge as belonging to the one person of the Son, who knows by his divine nature what his human nature learns and grows in (Luke 2:52); the passage does not ask us to settle how, only to confess that he knows.

**The Trinity and the resurrection.** Jesus says 'I will raise it up' (John 2:19). Elsewhere the New Testament says the Father raised him (Galatians 1:1; Acts 2:24) and associates the Spirit with the raising (Romans 8:11), and Jesus himself says, "I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (John 10:18). The historic doctrine that the external works of the Trinity are undivided explains these texts without setting them against one another: the one God raises the Son, and the Son, as God, raises himself.

**Covenant and fulfilment.** The two scenes are covenant theology in motion. The old covenant's purifying rites (John 2:6) and sanctuary (John 2:19) were true and God-given, but they were shadows (Hebrews 8:5; 9:11). In Christ the reality has come: the wine of the promised feast (Amos 9:13; Isaiah 25:6) and the temple not made with hands (Mark 14:58; Hebrews 9:11). A Reformed reading stresses continuity (the same God, the same promise) as well as discontinuity (the shadow gives way to the substance). John does not say the old was bad wine; he says the good wine was kept until now.

**Ecclesiology.** Because Christ's risen body is the true temple, those united to him by the Spirit are built into that temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22; 1 Peter 2:5). This is the ground for church purity: the cleansing of the temple is a pattern for Christ's continuing reformation of his church by his word.

**Soteriology.** John 2:23–25 introduces what Reformed theology has called 'temporary faith': an assent to Jesus prompted by what one sees, which does not rest on him and does not persevere (compare Matthew 13:20–21; John 6:66; 1 John 2:19). John's Gospel distinguishes such faith from the faith that continues in his word (John 8:31) and receives him (John 1:12).

**Scripture.** John 2:22 places 'the scripture' and 'the word which Jesus had said' side by side as objects of the same faith, and shows that the disciples read the Old Testament rightly only in the light of the risen Christ (compare Luke 24:27, 45). The hermeneutic this unit follows, reading Scripture by Scripture and the Old Testament toward Christ, is modelled here by the apostles themselves.

### 📖 Key Verses
> "Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come." (John 2:4)

*Exegetical note.* The idiom 'what have I to do with thee' (literally 'what to me and to you') occurs in the Old Testament and the Gospels with a range of force, from hostile (Mark 1:24, of demons; 2 Kings 3:13, Elisha to Israel's king) to a firm refusal of someone else's agenda without hostility (2 Samuel 16:10, David to the sons of Zeruiah). Context decides. Here it marks the Son's independence from human prompting; 'mine hour' ties even this domestic moment to the cross. The hour is the controlling category of John's plot.

> "And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece." (John 2:6)

*Exegetical note.* The phrase 'after the manner of the purifying' (literally 'according to the purification') is the interpretive key the narrator supplies. The noun *katharismos* (G2512, John 2:6) reappears in John 3:25 in the dispute about purifying between John's disciples and a Jew. The sign replaces the water of purification with the wine of the kingdom.

> "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11)

*Exegetical note.* 'Beginning' can mean first in a sequence or first in principle. Both are probably in view: the first sign is also the paradigm for the rest. The verb *ephanerōsen* (G5319, John 2:11, V-AAI-3S), 'manifested', is used again when the risen Jesus 'shewed himself' to his disciples by the sea (John 21:1, 14), so the same verb spans Jesus' self-revelation from the first sign to the last resurrection appearance John records.

> "And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up." (John 2:17)

*Exegetical note.* The KJV's 'hath eaten me up' follows the Textus Receptus and matches the tense of Psalm 69:9. Many modern editions of the Greek read a future here ('shall eat me up'), which points forward to the passion. Either way, John frames Jesus' zeal with a psalm of the righteous sufferer, and the context of the psalm makes the point: zeal for God's house will cost the zealous one his life.

> "Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." (John 2:19)

*Exegetical note.* The imperative 'Destroy' is commonly read by grammarians as a conditional or ironic imperative ('if you destroy', or 'go on, destroy'): Jesus is not commanding sin but foretelling what they will do. The shift from the word for the temple precincts in John 2:14–15 to the word for the sanctuary here is deliberate.

> "Then said the Jews, Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?" (John 2:20)

*Exegetical note.* The number is a historical anchor. Taking Herod's project as beginning about 20–19 BC, the statement dates this Passover to about AD 27–28. The misunderstanding also carries irony: the building they are proud of will be destroyed in AD 70, while the temple they will destroy will rise.

> "But he spake of the temple of his body." (John 2:21)

*Exegetical note.* A narrator's aside (the pronoun is emphatic, 'but he', that is, as distinct from them) that interprets the saying. The genitive 'the temple of his body' is best taken as identifying: the temple which is his body.

> "When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said." (John 2:22)

*Exegetical note.* The post-resurrection vantage point of the Gospel is openly acknowledged. This is not a weakness but a claim: the meaning of Jesus' words was given by the event itself and confirmed by Scripture.

> "Now when he was in Jerusalem at the passover, in the feast day, many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did." (John 2:23)

*Exegetical note.* 'Believed in his name' is a phrase John also uses of genuine faith (John 1:12), so the difference lies not in the vocabulary but in what follows. The participle 'beholding' (KJV 'when they saw') grounds the faith in watching the signs.

> "But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men, And needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man." (John 2:24–25)

*Exegetical note.* The imperfects ('was not entrusting', 'was knowing') describe Jesus' settled practice, not one moment. The verb 'testify' anticipates John's great theme of witness (John 5:31–47); Jesus needs no human witness about human beings.

### 📚 Scholarly Insight
- **Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*** (the tractates on John 2). Augustine reads the water as the Old Testament prophecies, which are turned to wine when Christ opens their meaning, and he famously takes the six waterpots as the six ages of the world. The first idea has real grounding in John 2:22; the second is allegory the text does not ask for. (Verify the tractate numbers before citing.)
- **John Chrysostom, *Homilies on the Gospel of John*.** Chrysostom suggests that Mary's request carried a natural maternal wish to see her son honoured, and that Jesus' answer gently corrects it. (Verify.) Whether or not one follows him, he takes seriously that Jesus' reply marks a real distance.
- **John Calvin, *Commentary on the Gospel According to John*.** Calvin reads Jesus' reply to Mary as a guard against giving her any authority over Christ's work, which he connects to later devotion to Mary. He also treats the temple cleansing in John 2 as distinct from the one the other Gospels place in the last week. (Verify the second point.)
- **J. C. Ryle, *Expository Thoughts on the Gospels* (John).** Ryle draws practical lessons: Christ's presence at a wedding honours marriage and lawful joy; the chapter's close warns that many profess faith who are not converted. He also reads John 2:4 as leaving no room for prayers to Mary. (Verify the last point.)
- **Leon Morris, *The Gospel According to John* (New International Commentary on the New Testament).** Morris argues that John and the Synoptics record two separate cleansings, weighing the differences of detail between the accounts.
- **D. A. Carson, *The Gospel According to John* (Pillar New Testament Commentary).** Carson also argues for two cleansings, stressing the differences in detail and John's explicit chronological markers. He reads the Cana sign as the replacement of Jewish purification with the new wine of the kingdom, and treats John 2:23–25 as an example of spurious or at least inadequate faith.
- **Raymond E. Brown, *The Gospel According to John* (Anchor Bible).** Brown, writing from a Roman Catholic and historical-critical standpoint, reads chapters 2–4 around the theme of Jesus replacing Jewish institutions, and holds that there was only one cleansing, which John has placed where it serves his theology. (Verify his view of which placement is historical.)

### ⚔️ Debate Corner
**The question: did Jesus cleanse the temple once or twice?** John places a cleansing at the first Passover of the ministry (John 2:13); Matthew, Mark and Luke place one in the final week (Matthew 21:12–13; Mark 11:15–17; Luke 19:45–46).

**Position 1: two cleansings.** Jesus cleansed the temple at the start of his ministry and again at the end. Holders (among them Calvin, Morris, Carson, and many conservative commentators) point out that the accounts differ in their details: John alone has the scourge, the oxen and sheep, 'my Father's house', and Psalm 69; the Synoptics have Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, 'den of thieves'. John's markers are explicitly chronological ('After this', John 2:12; the Passover 'at hand', John 2:13; forty-six years). The false witnesses at Jesus' trial remember a saying about destroying the temple (Mark 14:58) which no Synoptic Gospel records, and which fits well if it was spoken years earlier, as John reports. And it would not be surprising if the abuse returned after a first rebuke.

**Position 2: one cleansing, placed by John for theological reasons.** Many modern scholars (Brown among them) hold that the event happened once, near the end, as the Synoptics report, and that John moved it to the start as a programmatic statement of Jesus' mission. Holders point out that the Gospels do arrange material topically at times, that an act like this would likely have provoked the authorities to act at once (which fits the Synoptic sequence, Mark 11:18), and that the core of both accounts is the same event. Many who hold this view do not think it compromises the truthfulness of Scripture, since, they argue, John is not claiming a chronological sequence in the way a modern historian would.

**Position 3: one cleansing, early, as John reports.** A minority hold that John's placement is historical and that the Synoptics, which narrate only one Jerusalem visit in the ministry, placed the single cleansing in the only Jerusalem visit they tell. (Verify which modern scholars hold this.)

**The most consistent reading under Reformed hermeneutics.** Reformed interpretation reads each text in its own grammatical and historical sense, lets Scripture interpret Scripture, and receives each Gospel as fully truthful in what it asserts. By that standard Position 1 is the strongest. John's temporal markers here are not vague ('After this', a named Passover, a dated building programme), and the differences between the accounts in wording, Old Testament citation, and response go beyond what one would expect of the same event retold. The trial testimony of Mark 14:58 is a real point of contact that the two-cleansings view explains naturally. This is an argument, not a proof. Position 2 is held by some who are committed to the authority of Scripture and who argue that topical arrangement is not error, and it should not be caricatured as unbelief. But it has to treat John's chronological markers as something other than chronology, and the two-cleansings reading does not.

**⚠️ Pastoral Warning.** Two opposite dangers. The first is to treat this question as a test of orthodoxy, so that a sincere believer who holds a single cleansing is treated as suspect; that turns a matter of harmonisation into a boundary marker the confessions never made one. The second is to let critics persuade a group that the Gospels contradict each other here, and so to quietly lose confidence in the reliability of the Gospels. A teacher should show the group that careful, honest reasons exist for reading the accounts as two events, and then turn back to what both accounts teach: the Lord has come to his temple, and he means to purify it.

### 🔤 Original Language Deep Dive
**Believing and entrusting: *pisteuō* in John 2.** The verb *pisteuō*, 'to believe, to trust', appears 4 times in John 2, and the chapter's final lesson turns on it.

1. *episteusan* (G4100, John 2:11, V-AAI-3P): 'his disciples believed on him'. Aorist active indicative, third person plural, with the preposition *eis* ('into, on'), a construction characteristic of John for personal trust in Jesus.
2. *episteusan* (G4100, John 2:22, V-AAI-3P): 'they believed the scripture, and the word'. The same form, here with the dative: belief in the truth of what was spoken.
3. *episteusan* (G4100, John 2:23, V-AAI-3P): 'many believed in his name'. The same form again, with *eis to onoma*, 'into the name'.
4. *episteuen* (G4100, John 2:24, V-IAI-3S): 'Jesus did not commit himself unto them'. Imperfect active indicative, third person singular, with the reflexive pronoun: literally 'was not entrusting himself to them'.

**Cognates and semantic range.** The verb belongs with the noun *pistis*, faith, and the adjective *pistos*, faithful. Its range runs from believing that something is true, through trusting a person, to entrusting something to someone (as in John 2:24 and Luke 16:11). John never uses the noun *pistis*; he always uses the verb, which keeps faith active: something people do, or fail to do, in response to Jesus. That observation is common in the commentaries and is borne out by the concordance.

**Septuagint background.** According to the lexicon, *pisteuō* in the Greek Old Testament chiefly renders the Hebrew *aman* (H539) in its causative form, 'to trust, to rely on', as in Abraham's believing God (Genesis 15:6) and Israel's believing after the Exodus signs (Exodus 14:31). That background is instructive for John 2: in Exodus, signs led Israel to believe, yet the same generation fell in the wilderness. Sign-faith that did not persevere is an old story.

**The grammar of the wordplay.** The aorist 'believed' in John 2:23 summarises what the crowd did; the imperfect in John 2:24 describes Jesus' ongoing stance, and the parallel imperfect *eginōsken* (G1097, John 2:25, V-IAI-3S), 'he knew', gives its ground. Beware of overreading tense here: the aorist does not in itself mean the crowd's faith was momentary, and the imperfect does not in itself mean anything more than an ongoing or customary action. The contrast comes from the repetition of the verb and from John's narrative, not from the tenses alone.

**Two more words in the temple saying.** *lusate* (G3089, John 2:19, V-AAM-2P) is an aorist active imperative, second person plural, from *luō*, 'to loose', and by extension 'to break up, destroy'; the lexicon lists John 2:19 under that sense. *egerō* (G1453, John 2:19, V-FAI-1S) is a future active indicative, first person singular, 'I will raise'. Its partner in John 2:22, *ēgerthē* (G1453, John 2:22, V-API-3S), is aorist passive, which the KJV renders 'he was risen'. Some press the passive as a 'divine passive' (raised by the Father), but the aorist passive of this verb is often used intransitively ('he rose'), so the form alone cannot carry that weight. The doctrine of the Father raising the Son is well grounded elsewhere (Galatians 1:1); it does not need this form to bear it.

### 💡 Tip
**Read the narrator.** John's Gospel has an unusually active narrator. A disciplined hermeneutical habit is to list every narrator's comment in a passage (in John 2, verses 9, 11, 17, 21–22 and 24–25), treat them as the author's own reading of the events, and build the sermon's interpretive spine from them before consulting a commentary. This keeps you from importing a meaning John did not give and from missing the one he did.

### 🔧 Hack
**A sermon-prep workflow for a narrative chapter.** (1) Print the chapter from `tools/verse.py` and mark scene changes. (2) Mark the narrator's comments in one colour, Old Testament quotations and allusions in another. (3) Run `tools/greek.py` on those verses only and note the key words. (4) Use `tools/concordance.py` to trace one of those words through John. (5) Only then read two commentaries from different traditions (for this chapter, Carson and Brown) and note where they disagree and why. (6) Write your big idea in one sentence before you write the outline.

### 🎯 Teaching Angle
**Teaching John 2 to a Tier 2 group (60 minutes).** Structure the session around the phrase 'the good wine until now': (1) the old that was good (purifying water, temple, Passover); (2) the new that is better (the wine, the body raised); (3) the faith that recognises the difference (John 2:11 versus John 2:23–25). Give each small group one scene and have them report what the narrator says it means.

**The three toughest questions, and answers.**
1. *Was the wine at Cana alcoholic?* The text calls it 'good wine' and the governor compares it with what is served 'when men have well drunk', where the verb is *methusthōsin* (G3184, John 2:10), which the lexicon defines as being drunken. Most commentators across traditions therefore take it as ordinary fermented wine. Some Christians, especially in the temperance tradition, argue it was unfermented grape juice; that view has to work against the governor's words. Scripture praises wine as God's gift (Psalm 104:15) and forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). A group can hold both, and should respect members who abstain for reasons of conscience or recovery.
2. *Does Jesus' anger in the temple justify violence or anger in us?* Jesus acts as the Son in his Father's house, with an authority no disciple shares. His zeal was holy and costly to himself (Psalm 69:9), and John describes animals driven out, coins poured out and tables overturned, with no one said to be harmed. It teaches us to take the purity of worship seriously, not to take the law into our own hands.
3. *If Jesus knows what is in man, why did he later choose Judas?* John raises this himself (John 6:64, 70–71): Jesus knew from the beginning. His choosing Judas was not ignorance but part of the Father's purpose in the passion (John 13:18). Jesus' knowledge of hearts is not a reason to despair but a reason to be honest: the one who knows us fully is the one who calls us.

### 🎤 Preaching Titles
- The Good Wine Kept Until Now
- Zeal for Your House: When Jesus Comes to Church
- The Temple That Rose on the Third Day

### ✅ Action Step
**A 30-day deep study ending in a real delivery.**
- **Days 1–7: Text.** Read John 2 daily. Make your own translation notes using `tools/greek.py` for verses 4, 6, 11, 17, 19, and 23–25. List every narrator's comment.
- **Days 8–14: Canon.** Trace the temple theme from Exodus 25:8 and 40:34, through 1 Kings 8:10–11, Ezekiel 10:18 and 43:4, Malachi 3:1, John 2:19–21, 1 Corinthians 3:16, to Revelation 21:22. Write one page on how the story fits together.
- **Days 15–21: Debate.** Read the cleansing accounts side by side (John 2:13–22; Matthew 21:12–13; Mark 11:15–18; Luke 19:45–46). Read Carson or Morris and Brown on the question. Write a one-page summary of each position in words its holders would accept, then your own conclusion.
- **Days 22–27: Preparation.** Write a 20-minute lesson on one of the three Preaching Titles, with a clear big idea, three movements, and one concrete application.
- **Days 28–30: Delivery.** Teach it to the TONA group or a home group, or record it. Ask two listeners for written feedback: What was clear? What was confusing? Did I stay with the text? Revise your notes accordingly.

## 🔗 Cross-Tier Connectors

### 🔗 Golden Thread
In Jesus, God keeps the best until now: the wine of the promised feast and the temple where God and sinners meet are found in the crucified and risen Son, who knows us completely and calls for a faith that rests on him, not on the spectacle.

### 📊 Progress Map
- **Root:** Jesus reveals his glory at Cana and names his body as the true temple (John 2:11, 19–21).
- **Tier 1:** A sign is a pointer; bring empty jars to Jesus, do what he says, and trust him because of who he is.
- **Tier 2:** Read every verse in its setting: the hour, the jars of purification, Passover and the temple courts, the misunderstanding, and the narrator's comments; learn to spot sign-faith.
- **Tier 3:** Place the chapter in Christology, covenant fulfilment and the theology of the temple; weigh the one-or-two-cleansings debate; work with the Greek of John 2:23–25 and 2:19; deliver a lesson.

### 🧩 Unlock Moments
- **Root → Tier 1:** Realising that John calls the miracle a sign, so the question is never only 'what happened?' but 'what does this show about Jesus?'
- **Tier 1 → Tier 2:** Noticing that the jars were for Jewish purifying and that the temple saying is about his body: the chapter is about Jesus fulfilling and replacing the old ways of approaching God.
- **Tier 2 → Tier 3:** Seeing the same verb in John 2:23 and 2:24, many believed in him, but he did not entrust himself to them, and grasping that John is teaching the difference between faith in signs and faith in the Son.

## 🌀 Spiral

### 🔑 Follow-Up Topics
- The temple in the Bible: from Eden and the tabernacle to Christ, the church, and the new Jerusalem.
- The hour in John: why Jesus' death is his glorification.
- True and temporary faith: what John teaches about believing that does and does not save.

### ➡️ Next in John
Chapter 2 ends with a sentence about man and what is in him, and chapter 3 begins with a man. Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a ruler, impressed by the signs ("no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him" (John 3:2)), exactly the kind of believer John 2:23–25 describes. He comes by night, and Jesus tells him that seeing signs is not enough: he must be born again. The jars of purification and the temple have given way to Jesus; now we learn that the one who would enter his kingdom needs not reformed religion but new birth from above.
